analysis.title: The clean-tech turning point and why emissions could soon follow (Allianz Green Transition Tracker 2026)
key_insights: Second edition of the Green Transition Tracker covers 65 countries, 81% of global GHG emissions. 56 of 65 moved closer to net-zero benchmarks, with Progress Scores up 2.0 points on average. At the current pace the world reaches net-zero benchmark levels around 2064.

In 2025 renewables passed coal as the largest source of global electricity: 33.5% of generation vs coal's 33.2%. Renewables supplied 99% of new generation. Global GHG emissions growth slowed to 0.7% from 1.5% in both 2023 and 2024, and power-sector emissions fell 0.3%.

For 2026, global emissions are expected to be broadly stable and fossil-fuel CO2 emissions to fall about 0.5%, the first annual decline since 2020. Higher fossil-fuel prices and cheaper clean technology support the shift. A single down year does not establish a structural turning point.

Global clean-energy investment is projected to rise 6.5% to USD 2.2trn in 2026, against USD 1.2trn for fossil. Renewable generation spending falls 3.6% (USD 690bn to USD 665bn), mostly in China. Grid investment rises 20.8% and battery storage 35.9%.

Battery storage additions rose from about 2 GWh in 2015 to 307 GWh in 2025 as installed costs fell 91% to about USD 140/kWh. BEV share of new car registrations rose from 18.1% in Q3 2025 to 21.8% in Q3 2026. Heat pump sales remain weak because of high upfront costs and electricity-to-gas price ratios.

The Strait of Hormuz disruption and the Iran conflict raised diesel prices. Reproducing the increase through carbon pricing would need more than EUR 200/tCO2. Oil supply disruptions are expected to cut global oil demand by 2.4 mb/d (2.6%) in 2026.

EU: emissions fell only 0.2% in 2025 vs an average -4% a year previously. At the current pace the EU reaches net-zero-aligned levels in 2057, a seven-year gap. Transport is now the largest emitting sector at 25.6% of EU emissions. EU BEV registrations rose 32-56% y/y in the first three quarters of 2026, and BEVs were 30% of September registrations.

EU policy risks: proposed changes to the EU ETS may weaken near-term incentives, ETS2 (road transport and buildings, due 2028) is delayed, and fossil-fuel subsidies remain about 70% above pre-2022 levels after rising 170% to USD 204bn in the 2022 energy crisis.

US: Progress Score rose 1.2 points to 18.9, ranking 41st (from 40th). Emissions rose 2.2% in 2025, the second straight annual increase. Coal-fired generation rose 13%, and the power sector accounted for 51% of the emissions increase. BEV sales weakened after federal tax credits ended in September 2025, recovering to 6.3% of sales from a low of 4.3%.

US electricity demand is projected to rise more than 400 TWh (about 9%) by 2030. Data centers are expected to supply about 48% of the additional demand (about 210 TWh), vs 35% over the past five years. AI workloads add an estimated 23.6 MtCO2, about 15% of the emissions increase since 2023, and could quadruple by 2030.

China: emissions growth slowed to 0.06% in 2025 (0.9% in 2024, 3.7% in 2023), at 15,981 MtCO2eq. Coal-fired generation fell about 1.5% while electricity demand rose 5.1%. EVs are 53% of new car sales, displacing about 1 mb/d of oil in 2025. EVs could displace more than 4 mb/d by 2035 under IEA scenarios. Progress Score rose to 15.6, ranking 43rd.

India: emissions fell 0.2% in 2025 to 4,508 MtCO2eq, the first decline outside an economic contraction in 25 years, with GDP up about 7.6%. Progress Score rose 4.5 points to 14.6. The gain was partly from mild weather and strong monsoon hydropower.

India in 2026: coal generation rose nearly 10% y/y between April and August (13% in September) while hydropower fell 11% (20% in September). The IEA expects Indian electricity demand to grow 6.4% a year through 2030. Planned coal additions by 2035 may rise from 97 GW to 105-150 GW, which creates a risk of underused coal assets.

India's NDC targets a 47% cut in GDP emissions intensity by 2035 vs 2005 and a 60% non-fossil share of installed capacity, with no absolute emissions peak before 2035. India added about 51 GW of renewable capacity in fiscal 2025-26. Grid curtailment reached about 300 GWh in Q1 2026.

Colombia had the largest Progress Score gain (+16.5 points to 25), from a 25% hydropower rebound to 68.1 TWh and solar growth. Hydropower is still about 94% of low-carbon generation, which leaves the system exposed to drought. Australia is the world's third-largest utility battery market, with 2.0 GW (5.1 GWh) commissioned in 2025 and a 82% renewable share target for 2030.

Carbon dioxide removal: ambitious pathways need about 8.8 GtCO2 a year by 2050, against national pledges of 3.6 Gt (41% coverage, a 5.2 Gt gap). Reported novel CDR was 2.04 MtCO2 in 2025, with biochar and BECCS 97% of it and DACCS 0.0015 Mt. Novel CDR capacity of 8.4 Mt by 2030 compares with about 70 Mt required (12%). A ten-year delay in cuts raises the 2100 removal need to 23.6 Gt, about 54% higher.

CDR contract prices range from USD 61/tCO2 (biomass direct storage) to USD 1,331 (direct ocean removal). Biochar averages USD 136, BECCS USD 220 and DACCS USD 516. At USD 150-400/tCO2, 3.5 Gt of annual novel removals in 2050 would cost USD 525bn-1.4trn a year.

The dated global wind and solar pipeline adds 509 TWh/yr in 2027, falling to 351 TWh/yr in 2028, 238 in 2029 and 202 in 2030, totaling about 1,300 TWh/yr. The US (215 TWh/yr), China (136), India (132) and Australia (129) lead. The data is a dated inventory, not a forecast. It excludes distributed solar, which understates China.

Economic scenario: wind and solar additions imply an average GDP-per-capita growth gain of 0.21pp a year across the top 30 countries for 2027-2030 (the model coefficient is not statistically significant, p=0.35), and an average CPI reduction of about 0.04pp a year. The effects are small and concentrated in small power systems.

Near-term risks to transition: rising electricity demand from AI and data centers (could add about 0.6% to global emissions by 2030), grid congestion and permitting delays, financing costs, critical-mineral price rebounds, export controls and El Niño. AI efficiency gains could cut emissions by up to 2.6% by 2035.

sector_views.rationale: Investment in grids (+20.8%) and storage (+35.9%) is growing fastest in 2026 as renewables generation spending dips. Falling battery costs and high fuel prices support EV adoption.
Global renewable investment is expected to fall from USD 690bn to USD 665bn in 2026, mostly in China, though renewables supplied 99% of new generation in 2025.

Coal lost its lead in global generation in 2025, but US coal generation rose 13% and India's rose about 10% in April-August 2026 on demand growth. Coal and gas/LNG investment in the US more than tripled from 2024 levels.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Slowdown from 1.5% in 2023 and 2024, driven by a 0.3% fall in power-sector emissions.
Would be the first annual decline since 2020, driven partly by higher fossil-fuel prices and clean-energy deployment.
Growth is led by grids and storage while renewable generation spending falls 3.6%.

macro_indicators.indicator: Global oil demand change from supply disruptions
macro_indicators.interpretation: Hormuz-related supply disruption cuts oil demand and strengthens the case for electrification.
Energy-related emissions rose only 0.6%, so emissions are decoupling from growth, though incompletely.
Second consecutive annual increase, driven by a 13% rise in coal-fired generation.
Data centers are expected to account for about 48% of the additional demand.
IEA forecast. Solar is expected to meet about half of the added demand and coal about a quarter.
Fell despite 5.1% electricity demand growth, so clean power is displacing coal rather than just meeting new demand.
Well below the previous average annual reduction of 4%.

macro_indicators.indicator: Global BEV share of new car registrations
macro_indicators.interpretation: Up from 18.1% in Q3 2025, supported by higher fuel prices and falling BEV costs.

macro_indicators.indicator: Model-implied CPI effect of wind and solar additions
macro_indicators.interpretation: Small disinflationary effect from lower wholesale power prices. It is a scenario, not a forecast.

risk_factors: Rising electricity demand from AI and data centers could add about 0.6% to global emissions by 2030 if met with fossil generation, especially gas.
Grid bottlenecks, connection queues and permitting delays slow renewable deployment and raise curtailment.
A reversal in fossil-fuel prices combined with persistent fossil subsidies could weaken electrification incentives.
Higher interest rates and inflation raise financing costs for capital-intensive clean projects, especially in emerging markets.
Critical-mineral price rebounds and export controls could raise battery costs.
Policy uncertainty: delayed EU ETS2, proposed changes to post-2030 EU ETS, reduced US clean-energy support, and China and India targets that do not cap absolute emissions.
A developing El Niño could raise cooling demand, weaken hydropower and raise fossil-fuel use.
India's hydropower and weather dependence, and possible coal overinvestment.
Carbon removal scale-up gap: BECCS project delays and cancellations in 2025 from uncertain demand and no long-term purchase agreements.
geopolitical: Iran conflict and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz raised diesel prices and fossil-fuel prices, which strengthens the case for electrification and EV adoption.
US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and the end of federal clean-energy tax credits create policy uncertainty for clean investment.
Trade fragmentation, tariffs and export controls on critical minerals pose cost and supply-chain risks for clean technology.
EU ETS2 delay and proposed easing of carbon-market tightening after 2030.

tension_points.bull_case: Renewables supplied 99% of new generation in 2025, emissions growth slowed to 0.7%, fossil CO2 is projected to fall about 0.5% in 2026, and China emissions growth has nearly stopped.
tension_points.bear_case: A single year of declining emissions does not establish a structural turning point. AI and data-center demand, grid bottlenecks and fossil lock-ins (US coal +13%, India coal +10% in April-August 2026) could slow progress.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Clean electricity supply failing to keep pace with demand growth, so that gas and coal fill the gap. A reversal in fossil-fuel prices would also weaken the electrification incentive.

tension_points.bull_case: AI-enabled efficiency gains could cut emissions by up to 2.6% by 2035, and data-center demand is spurring grid and storage investment.
tension_points.bear_case: AI and data centers could add about 0.6% to global emissions by 2030, and AI workloads' US emissions could quadruple by 2030.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Whether the electricity supply is carbon-intensive and whether efficiency gains outweigh the footprint.

theme_stances.evidence: Rising electricity demand and infrastructure bottlenecks pose the greatest risk
